### Executive summary
Essential Newborn Care Course second edition provides policy-makers and programme managers, faculty in academic institutions, educational course organizers and facilitators with:
- guidance on implementing Essential Newborn Care Course (ENCC) second edition as part of broader efforts around health worker education and newborn service delivery;
- a repository for access to all Essential Newborn Care Course educational materials and implementation resources; and
- support for the principles of essential newborn care as the foundation for quality care of all newborns.
##### **Transforming the approach to education with Essential Newborn Care Course second edition**
Ending preventable deaths of newborns and setting them on a path to thrive is the goal of essential newborn care. Achieving this goal requires addressing the global burden of newborn deaths and stillbirths, the numbers and competencies of the health workforce, and the gap between knowledge and performance in the clinical setting. Essential Newborn Care Course second edition addresses all these topics and establishes the foundation of quality care for all newborns, whether healthy and well-grown or small and sick. Essential Newborn Care Course second edition integrates WHO guidelines, recommendations and quality of care standards with a newborn-centred perspective, emphasizing the right to respectful, nurturing care. It is competency-based and incorporates contemporary educational methods including peer learning, simulation for skill-building and team performance, reflective debriefing and integration with facility-based quality improvement.
##### **Planning and implementation of health worker education to improve outcomes**
The aim of the ten steps for planning and implementing health worker education is to improve newborn outcomes.
1. At the national level, establish a functional maternal/newborn/child health alliance with public, private and nongovernmental partners.
2. Form a functional working group at the national level for advocacy, planning, implementation and monitoring around educational activities.
3. Decide on an education implementation strategy.
4. Provide appropriately adapted learning materials simultaneously with equipment and supplies to deliver essential newborn care.
5. Identify and support local leaders and champions.
VII

6. Strengthen local systems for regular education, frequent refreshers, regular debriefing after clinical care and audits.
7. Support the function of facility-level quality improvement teams.
8. Collect, report and use local data on a standardized set of basic process indicators for care and newborn outcomes.
9. Develop a system for bidirectional reporting and feedback to/from all levels of the health system and working group.
10. Engage and empower health workers, families and the broader community in the initiative.
##### **Linking education to functional health care delivery systems**
Achieving the goals of newborn survival and quality of survival requires not just educational effectiveness and efficiency, but also local implementation of best practices in health care delivery. A health systems approach with simultaneous action on policy, administration, finances, infrastructure, human resources, data management, equipment and supply logistics is necessary to support clinical service delivery. High-quality newborn care also demands linkage of maternal and newborn care in the facility; this includes building a common knowledge base and skill set among health workers, as well as communication and teamwork. The physical infrastructure of health facilities and organization of transport systems should support a zero-separation model. Finally, successful local implementation of essential newborn care forms the foundation for special care of small and/or sick newborns: Essential Newborn Care Course second edition develops the necessary assessment and reassessment skills, and the ability to formulate a plan that emphasizes kangaroo mother care and provides support for breastfeeding and breast-milk feeding.

### Introduction
The first edition of the WHO Essential Newborn Care Course was published in 2010. The second edition integrates WHO guidelines, recommendations, quality-of care standards and materials updated since 2010. The educational materials are newborn-centred, addressing the newborn’s right to high-quality, respectful care. The setting of the course has been shifted from the classroom to health facilities and varied contexts in which newborns receive care, including humanitarian situations.
##### **The purpose of this document is to:**
- guide countries and programmes in implementing the Essential Newborn Care Course second edition as part of broader efforts around health worker education and newborn service delivery;
- provide a repository for access to all educational materials that make up the Essential Newborn Care Course second edition as well as implementation resources; and
- articulate the principles of essential newborn care as the foundation for quality care of all newborns, whether healthy or small and/or sick.
##### **The document targets a broad audience of users**
- Policy-makers and programme managers at national, subnational and local levels (including governmental and nongovernmental organizations) will find policy and strategy rationale, practical guidance on programme planning and implementation and considerations for health care delivery systems (sections 1-3).
- Faculty in academic institutions and persons delivery health worker education programmes will find specific sections on the planning and implementation of essential newborn care in their particular settings (section 2).
- Essential Newborn Care Course organizers and facilitators (from facilities, academic institutions, professional associations and the community) will find guidance on implementation, monitoring and evaluation as well as direct links to educational materials (section 2).

##### **How this Essential Newborn Care Course, second edition was developed**
Development of the Essential Newborn Care Course second edition started in 2017 with collaboration between WHO and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). In 2019 the WHO Regional Office for Africa coordinated field-testing of Essential Newborn Care 1 and 2 in the United Republic of Tanzania.
A scoping review identified all guidelines, standards, indicators and materials related to newborn care, newborn-centred care, newborn survival, morbidity, disability and development that had been updated since the first edition in 2010.
New educational methodologies field-tested as part of the WHO Essential Childbirth Care Course in Telangana, India, in 2020 were integrated into the ENCC, and additional structured simulations linked to performance outcomes were added.
Online review and virtual testing of the materials under development in 2022 involved clinical educators and practitioners in Namibia, Lesotho, Nigeria and Kenya. Structured feedback from experts and participants was collated and incorporated into the thematic modules, assessments and implementation guidance for countries.
Face-to-face field-testing of the thematic modules was carried out in 2023 in Nigeria, prompting development of new material on data collection and use and extensive revision of facilitator guidance. Additional fieldtesting with both pre-service and in-service participants took place later in 2023 in India, which further informed facilitator and implementation resources.

### Transforming the approach to education with Essential Newborn Care Course second edition
#### 1.1 Addressing the situation
Ending the preventable deaths of newborns and setting them on the pathway to thriving is the goal of essential newborn care. Achieving this goal requires addressing:
Global burden of disease – Each day more than 6000 neonates, 5000 stillbirths and 700 women die from causes related to pregnancy and birth according to 2023 estimates ( _1,2_ ).
Essential newborn care directly addresses the high proportion of deaths that occur around childbirth. Providing stabilization and life-saving interventions such as immediate drying and skin-to-skin contact to avoid hypothermia, delayed umbilical cord clamping and early initiation of breastfeeding keep newborns healthy. Basic neonatal resuscitation directly addresses newborns who are not breathing at birth, reducing potential misclassification as stillbirths and preventing disability from delayed intervention. Kangaroo mother care addresses the primary needs of many low-birthweight and preterm newborns (nutrition, warmth, prevention of infection, nurturing care) and extends these benefits through the first month after birth.
Number and competencies of health workers – An estimated shortfall of 11.1 million health workers by 2030 is compounded by not all health workers having the needed competencies ( _3,4_ ).
Essential newborn care addresses the core competencies for providing maternal/newborn care in midwifery, nursing, and medical and community health curricula. Preparing students with knowledge and skills before they assume responsibility for clinical care, then reinforcing their learning with fully aligned orientation and refresher education in the health facility most efficiently maintains skills and competencies and fosters interprofessional teamwork.

**1. Transforming the approach to education**
Know-do gap – What health workers know is not always reflected in what they do. Of 8.6 million unnecessary deaths/year, 5 million are due to poor quality care and 3.6 million to non-utilisation of health care ( _5_ ).
Education in essential newborn care provides the framework for identifying gaps in quality care, and Essential Newborn Care Course second edition provides reliable methods for pinpointing quality improvement priorities that lead to a change in performance. Education based in the facility can result in improved availability of equipment and supplies, better workflow, more complete and accurate recording of data, as well as more responsive use of data.
Preventable deaths of newborns are often related to acute situations at birth and problems in the first days. The life of the newborn depends on the competencies of the health worker who is present and the facility’s readiness to deliver care.
Does the health worker understand the life-threatening situation?
Does the health worker know what to do and how to do it?
Can the health worker deliver the necessary care in the facility?

**1. Transforming the approach to education**
#### 1.2 Meeting the goal of ending preventable deaths
The essential newborn care approach serves as the foundation of quality care for all newborns. Whether healthy and well-grown or small and sick, all newborns need skilled attention at birth, a clean and safe environment, warmth, adequate nutrition, and prompt recognition and management of problems. However, essential newborn care alone is not sufficient to attain the goal of ending preventable newborn deaths. Essential care of the newborn must be linked to quality care of pregnant and parturient women and include scale-up of care for small and sick newborns in order to end preventable maternal and newborn deaths. Sustainable Development Goal targets for maternal health and child mortality and Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP) global, national and subnational targets for neonatal mortality and stillbirths set benchmarks for ending preventable maternal and newborn deaths ( _6,7_ ).
Targets for 2030
- SDG Target 3.1 – to reduce the global maternal mortality ratio to less than 70 per 100 000 live births
- SDG Target 3.2 – to reduce neonatal mortality to at least as low as 12 per 1000 live births and under-five mortality to at least as low as 25 per 1000 live births
- ENAP Target for stillbirth – to reduce stillbirths at 28 weeks or more of gestation to 12 or less per 1000 live births
Essential Newborn Care Course second edition directly addresses the need to educate more health workers, equip them with not only knowledge but also skills, and translate their knowledge and skills into performance and improved outcomes. It is designed for all health workers who care for newborns – midwives, nurses, physicians (medical officers, paediatricians, obstetricians) and other cadres, including auxiliaries and community health workers. Essential Newborn Care 1 begins with care in the first 60 minutes: Immediate Care and Helping Babies Breathe at Birth. Essential Newborn Care 2 continues with care from 60 to 90 minutes up to and including discharge from the facility and the first month: Assessment and Continuing Care. Three crosscutting modules address the foundation for quality in all newborn care and ten thematic modules explore specific issues.
The competencies, infrastructure, equipment and commodities required can also serve to reinforce the framework for RMNCH planning and service delivery. Successful implementation of Essential Newborn Care Course second edition demands country-led commitment through policy, guidelines, protocols, curricula and funding in combination with follow-up to foster local accountability and ownership. Each country needs to identify its own gaps, including disaggregation of data to highlight subnational conditions, so that education supports defined service delivery packages and patient outcome goals. Context, existing systems and available financial resources will influence how health worker education is adopted and institutionalized.

#### 1.4 Incorporating contemporary educational methods
Essential Newborn Care Course second edition integrates the contemporary WHO Learning Strategy and is competency-based, following the WHO Global Competency Framework for Universal Health Coverage (UHC).
- The WHO Learning Strategy has as its principles to:
- achieve global, national and individual goals for public health through a culture of lifelong learning;
- expand learning ecosystems through evidence-based approaches to support lifelong learning in health;
- aim for equity, design for competency and implement at scale in learning organizations;
- engage a broad health workforce (clinical service delivery, public health, emergency) and address the health literacy of individuals; and
- promote equity, capacity, transparency, participation and excellence.

**1. Transforming the approach to education**
The global competency framework for UHC identifies an approach to education pathways that emphasizes the domains of people-centredness, decision-making, communication, collaboration, evidence-informed practice and personal conduct. This approach is reflected in Essential Newborn Care competencies for participants and Essential Newborn Care competencies for facilitators that accompany the educational materials.
Essential Newborn Care Course second edition is built upon the most current science- and evidence-informed educational methods. Field-testing and implementation trials have demonstrated high learner satisfaction, confidence and increased knowledge and skills scores. It begins with health worker education but extends beyond the classroom to maintain and build skills, change performance in daily delivery of care, identify gaps in quality, make changes that result in improved health outcomes, and institutionalize a culture of continued learning and improvement.
By following the circle of learning and improvement (Fig. 2), Essential Newborn Care Course second edition aims to build competencies that save lives and help all newborns reach their full potential.

Education focuses on assessment, decision-making and skills. Flexible materials (print, digital, online) and educational tools (mannequins, models) permit on-site education, ongoing refresher practice, and scalability at low cost. Although education may result in demonstrated improvement in skills, often there is decay in skills over time and no change in performance in the clinical setting ( _8_ ).
###### **In order to translate skills into performance, there is a need to:**
- practise frequently in the real setting;
- feel supported by leaders in the health facility; and
- gain everyone’s participation in education, even the most senior doctors, midwives and nurses.

**1. Transforming the approach to education**
##### **Importance of refresher practice**
Establishing a routine of regular, brief practice maintains proficiency in life-saving skills. Designated skill areas in the labour ward provide access to educational materials and facilitate frequent practice. Institution of routine low-dose, high-frequency practice in several Tanzanian hospitals resulted in a change in resuscitation performance, with a 25% reduction in stillbirths and 40–80% reduction in very early neonatal mortality. However, starting ventilation late and pausing ventilation frequently were still associated with unfavourable outcomes ( _8,9_ ).
###### **In order to improve performance, there is a need to:**
- practise with feedback to achieve skills mastery, not just maintenance; and
- improve clinical equipment and organization to ease the burden
- for health workers and help them provide care efficiently.

##### **Low-dose, high-frequency practice focused in response to clinical outcomes**
Collecting data on process and outcome measures identifies gaps in performance and workflow as well as skills technique. Customizing educational content to address observed gaps creates change efficiently. Charting performance and outcomes of resuscitation monthly by using statistical process control methods led to an increase in perinatal survival directly correlated with low-dose, high-frequency practice in Nepal. Nevertheless, ventilation started late in some cases ( _10,11_ ).
###### **In order to improve performance further, there is a need to:**
- continue individual or peer-to-peer practice plus clinical feedback; and
- practise team function and communication, including nonjudgemental reflective debriefing.

**1. Transforming the approach to education**
##### **Simulation in teams combined with low-dose, high-frequency practice**
Regular team simulations led by local facilitators lead to improved team functioning. Culture change that supports regular, independent refresher practice at skills stations maintains individual skills. Collection of clinical performance data from observers or mobile applications individualizes performance feedback. Developing a system of team simulation helped improve coordination and communication issues and resolve system barriers so that the median time to ventilation dropped from 100 to 55 seconds and fresh stillbirths decreased significantly in a network of Tanzanian hospitals ( _12,13_ ).
###### **In order to maintain performance, there is a need to:**
- continue to address observed gaps and barriers in the system; and
- incorporate new personnel into team simulations.
Faculty prepare for practical sessions and simulations in the field linked to handover of mobile clinics, Hayan, Philippines. © Helenlouise Taylor
##### **Mentoring and in situ coaching for continued care skills in the facility**
In addition to team simulations, coaching and mentoring in the health facility can maintain and improve the performance of many skills that are part of continued care in the facility. Staff coaching, quality improvement assessments and changes in hospital protocols and environments were associated with improved care at delivery, rates of early and prolonged skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding in several countries in the Asia-Pacific region ( _14–16_ ). The duration of uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact correlated directly with the rate of early initiation of breastfeeding through 90 minutes after birth and exclusive breastfeeding at discharge following both vaginal and caesarean birth.
###### **In order to maintain performance, there is a need to:**
- continue to address observed gaps and barriers in the system; and
- Incorporate new personnel into mentorship and coaching activities.

# **2**
### Planning and implementation of health worker education to improve outcomes
- 2.1 At the national level, establish a functional maternal/newborn/child health alliance with public, private and nongovernmental partners
Leadership is central to the coordination and scale necessary to achieve impact from educational interventions. Even more, national leadership underpins institutionalization of the processes necessary to sustain that impact. Resource mobilization for education may require agreements among the government, public health partners and donors. Revision or adoption of policies and programme structures supporting education, as well as clinical and operational guidelines and protocols, helps to accelerate and make sustainable change at the subnational and facility level. High-level advocacy and communication create ownership and commitment throughout the country.
Although most countries have such a maternal/newborn/child health alliance, its functionality and representation may need to be renewed or strengthened. Planning to improve essential newborn care should extend across national planning and budgeting for reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health (RMNCH), nutrition, universal health coverage (UHC), quality improvement programmes, and medical and allied professional training. Coordination of maternal and newborn educational activities and programming addressing care around birth recognizes their interdependence and represents an efficient use of resources.
Regional alliances of several countries aligned by geography and/or language can address common gaps and goals and share implementation experiences. Regional efforts can provide important momentum for initial dissemination and a collaborative mechanism for sharing facilitator expertise, translations, educational data tracking, and programming for humanitarian settings and marginalized populations. Regional administrative structures and meetings of UN agencies, professional organizations, and public health and medical societies can be engaged in support of ENCC dissemination and replication.

#### 2.2 Form a functional working group at the national level for advocacy, planning, implementation and monitoring of educational activities
Central to the success of educational programming is a well-defined national plan based on a comprehensive RMNCH perspective, informed by situational assessment, accountable for achievable goals and timelines, and overseen by a working group at the national level. Key leadership from the Ministry of Health should be complemented by members from other ministries, such as the Ministry of Education. Advisory group representation should be broad and include professional associations and health-care professionals (nurses, midwives, paediatricians, obstetricians and anesthetists) from public and private sectors, frontline health workers (including community health workers) and student representatives, parents and community members. Stakeholders bring a broad range of considerations that reflect the real situation in the country, and they build consensus, ownership and commitment to the plan.
As a first step, the national working group will generally assess the current status of essential newborn care implementation and identify gaps in the current system. Review of available data sources addressing the major causes of neonatal morbidity and mortality will guide the prioritization of educational interventions. Data sources may include the national Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP), national and subnational HMIS coverage data; national and subnational mapping of mortality, morbidity, disability and effective coverage of maternal and newborn interventions (Countdown 2030), health facility and population-based surveys (MICS and DHS), and annual hospital implementation plans and reviews for Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC). If these data are not available, a situation analysis and/or health facility surveys using validated instruments can provide valuable insights.
Surveying existing policies, guidelines, protocols and educational materials serves to highlight potential Essential Newborn Care Course connections with ongoing activities and to re-align national treatment guidelines, policies or professional competencies if necessary. There may be an opportunity to establish or review and update performance standards for essential newborn care. In addition to revising in-service educational materials, the working group should promote the review and alignment of pre-service curricula.
Setting specific goals for ENCC implementation involves defining where you are and where you want to be. The goals should reflect the identified health priorities as well as the resources available.
Current programming can be leveraged to support ENCC implementation to make use of available resources while identifying potential additional resources for education. Targeting outcomes that have shown little improvement opens the way for large gains and may suggest that the plan should focus on certain conditions, population groups or geographical areas. To accompany the educational goals, a financial plan ought to be developed to address not only initial dissemination, but continued implementation of educational programming and institutionalization of structures that assure sustainability.
Oversight of the dissemination and implementation process as well as of educational and clinical outcomes constitutes the long-term activity of the working group. Adherence to the performance and timeline

#### 2.3 Decide on an education implementation strategy
The strategy for implementing the national plan for the Essential Newborn Care Course accounts for all levels in the health system, public and private health care delivery facilities and academic institutions, and the range of health workers providing care around birth; it links with systems of quality improvement and continuing professional development and/or accreditation. The expectation should be that all health workers who care for newborns have current competencies in their scope of practice. Essential Newborn Care Course implementation may be integrated into an existing strategy or function to update a previous strategy. Implementation may proceed in a cascade from national to facility level or it may be phased geographically or prioritized by groups with the greatest need or lowest health indicators. The strategy should build capacity at all levels by promoting high-quality facilitation and high coverage with education. Capacity-building includes champions who lead educational efforts, facilitators, health workers, and women and families. Capacity-building extends beyond ENCC to other educational interventions by strengthening leadership and organizational skills, pedagogical methods, the knowledge base and health literacy.
In order to achieve population-level and sustainable impact, the implementation strategy must include both public and private health facilities providing newborn services. While in-service education requirements may be set at the national level for public facilities, private health facilities may follow guidance from accrediting bodies or staff may comply with continuing professional development requirements for licensing or certification. Interprofessional in-service education should emphasize team functioning in the care of newborns, and their mothers and families. This includes nursing, midwifery, medical and allied health professionals, as well as other cadres caring for newborns and mothers during childbirth and the first month of life (e.g. birth attendants, auxiliary midwives or auxiliary nurses). Those who supervise the care of newborns, such as medical officers, paediatricians, obstetricians, and neonatologists, also need good practical knowledge of ENCC materials and current guidelines so they can effectively supervise and improve the quality of care as part of their routine daily work.
Pre-service education using ENCC content and methods is vital to prepare those who will care for newborns with the knowledge, skills, and competencies they will need before they assume responsibility for patients.
Essential Newborn Care Course provides an educational framework that can first be built during pre-service education, strengthened during orientation and in-service education, and adapted to become process and outcome indicators for quality improvement in the delivery of clinical care. Selected ENCC content can be used to reinforce ongoing educational programming for a variety of cadres, including skilled birth attendants, community health workers, and auxiliary nurses and midwives. Integration of essential newborn care into midwifery pre-service education curricula is vital to achieving the core competencies, as defined by the International Confederation of Midwives.

##### **In-service education**
Essential Newborn Care Course at a Glance provides detailed guidance for facilitators conducting educational sessions in health facilities. Essential Newborn Care Course is designed to be taught in many different environments where newborns receive care – in hospitals or health centres, in delivery rooms and postnatal wards at the community level, and in humanitarian situations. Experience in teaching ENCC has shown that participants are more likely to put new knowledge and skills into practice if they learn and follow up in their normal working environment. They are also more likely to notice gaps and improvements that they can make themselves as part of quality improvement, such as reorganizing the delivery room to ensure safety, privacy and ease of working. Where participants are widely dispersed geographically and patient volumes are low, planners may consider grouping participants geographically in one health facility and rotating educational sessions to the others each month or quarter, with facilitators travelling to minimize travel costs.

Clinical practice sessions in ENCC rely on having newborns and mothers receiving care under routine facility conditions at the time of observation. Facilities with low delivery volumes will need to adapt by teaching small groups of participants. Clinical practice is ideally carried out with access to the delivery area, postnatal areas, kangaroo mother care beds and outpatient newborn clinic.
ENCC materials can be used to provide a uniform and comprehensive educational foundation for all perinatal staff. All health workers who care for mothers and newborns during labour, delivery and the postnatal period should participate in training over time.
Timing of educational sessions can be adjusted to ensure that all staff (including those who work nights and weekends) are included. The materials are suitable for orientation of recently graduated health workers and experienced health workers who are new to newborn care. The framework for evaluation/decision/ action and essential newborn skills can be covered in concentrated learning sessions of two or three days. Refresher education can be structured as periodic short sessions of several minutes, a few hours or a half day distributed over time. A designated education space fosters short, frequent and regular skill practice sessions by individuals, peer-to-peer learning and team simulation. In order not to disrupt clinical care, sessions should be conducted with a small number of health workers and repeated. Staff identified by facilitators as having good skills can be mentored to facilitate for their colleagues in order to lighten the task and ensure sustainability. Self-reflection and debriefing after resuscitations, critical incidents, near-miss events, and discussions of morbidity or mortality can be especially effective learning opportunities. Patient care handovers and mentorship sessions also provide opportunities for low-dose, high-frequency refresher education. Periodic audits, such as Maternal Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR) and case reviews with analysis of systems issues and changes are additional opportunities for skills refreshers and even simulation. Regular (weekly or monthly) analysis of clinical outcomes in the facility can be used to inform and customize the educational focus.
Costing and budget allocation should address both the scale-up of in-service education and annual recurrent programming. Funds should be available to cover expenses of materials and equipment as well as facilitator/ organizer time. However, if opportunities are used within existing systems, such as updating skills at existing supportive supervision or integrated outreach visits, additional costs for improvement in newborn care can be marginal. In situ education in health facilities significantly reduces costs associated with travel, per diems and fees paid for educational sessions outside the health facility.

# **3**
### Linking education to functional health care delivery systems
#### 3.1 Linking education to functional delivery of essential newborn care
The Utstein formula for survival (Fig. 4) offers a framework for improving health care systems and understanding variability in clinical outcomes among sites and countries ( _18_ ). The formula proposes that patient outcome is a product of three interacting factors: medical science (guideline quality), educational efficiency (knowledge translation to health workers) and local implementation (actual delivery of health care). Although originally proposed relative to cardiac arrest, the formula can be modified for newborn survival and quality of survival outcomes. When any factor in the equation is lacking, the overall result diminishes. When two or more factors are lacking, the multiplier effect produces a dramatically diminished patient outcome. Although strong evidence supports the key interventions for essential newborn care (medical science), both the education of health workers (educational efficiency) and actual provision of those key interventions to newborns (local implementation) are often lacking. Improvement in educational efficiency to transmit best practices and local implementation will improve newborn outcomes – not just survival, but also quality of survival.

High-quality newborn care also demands linkage of maternal and newborn care in the facility, family and community involvement and support, and a post-discharge follow-up system at the facility and at home. Resources such as the WHO Guide for conducting national and subnational programme reviews for maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health _(19)_ and the accompanying programme review data tool can help accelerate widespread and successful implementation.

**Essential newborn care incorporates multiple evidence-based interventions** identified as central not only to survival but also to supporting health and human development ( _20_ ). This was noted in the report of the Lancet Commission on Optimizing Child Health and Human Development ( _4_ ).
“Structural reforms are more likely to improve service quality substantially and at scale than are micro-level efforts. Promising approaches include governing for quality (e.g. leadership, expert management and learning systems), redesigning service delivery to maximize outcomes, and empowering families to better care for children and to demand quality care from health and social systems.”
Strengthening the health-care system to provide essential newborn care creates the necessary solid foundation upon which to build coordinated perinatal services and more specialized neonatal services.

**Essential newborn care course - second edition**
#### 3.2 Linking newborn and maternal care in health worker education and service delivery
Essential newborn care does not stand alone; care of the newborn is closely linked with care of the pregnant woman and mother. All disciplines and cadres caring for the newborn should integrate competencies for essential newborn care into their curricula. Interprofessional education that embraces midwives, obstetricians, labour and delivery and postpartum nurses, medical officers, obstetricians and paediatricians reinforces a common knowledge base and shared skill set, and also promotes good communication and teamwork ( _21, 22_ ). Preparation of community health workers in essential newborn care is especially important to ensure continuation of best practices through the first weeks and months after birth.
The process of quality improvement around essential newborn care often points to changes in either intrapartum or postnatal care. Although essential newborn care addresses basic neonatal resuscitation, primary prevention of intrapartum-related events requires collaboration with those providing care to the pregnant woman. Achieving the goal of zero separation of mother and newborn mandates parallel capabilities in maternal and newborn service delivery to avoid referral of one member of the dyad. The physical infrastructure of health facilities should support a zero-separation model. When referral of either the woman or newborn is necessary, there should be purposeful referral to a facility that can provide the needed services and, ideally, transport of mother and newborn together with continued medical support. Postnatal follow-up of mother and newborn together is a potential strategy to improve disproportionately low rates of neonatal follow-up.

**Essential newborn care course - second edition**
#### 3.3 Essential newborn care as a foundation for small and sick newborn care
Successful local implementation of essential newborn care is the foundation for extending its principles towards providing special care for small and sick newborn infants. Essential Newborn Care Course second edition incorporates the fundamentals of kangaroo mother care and in-depth resources for both thermal support and support of breastfeeding and breast-milk feeding of preterm and small newborns. Essential Newborn Care Course second edition develops assessment and reassessment skills, and the ability to formulate a plan of care for a facility stay – the basis of safe and individualized special newborn care. Without the fundamentals of strong perinatal and essential newborn care, more advanced interventions such as CPAP, infection management and treatment for other conditions often fail to achieve their intended impact.
